Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : BM2300 : Bioprocess Engineering - I { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Basic concepts of process calculations, Fundamentals of material and energy balance for processes with/without chemical reaction. Simultaneous mass and energy balance in flow and without flow conditions. Microbial growth, batch, fed-batch and continuous growth, Nutritional requirements for growth and product formation. Medium design and optimization. Types of sterilization, thermal death kinetics of microorganism. Heat sterilization of liquid medium in batch and continuous mode. Air sterilization. Different types of bioreactors, configuration of Bioreactors and their main components. Modes of bioreactor operation. Fermentaion definition, inoculum development. Various types of Fermentation, submerged fermentation, aerobic and anaerobic fermentation. Overview of biosynthetic mechanisms. Metabolic stoichiometry.

Course Objective

1 .

Basic knowledge about bioprocessing of industrially important products

Course Outcome

1 .

The students will be able to explain the bioprocessing of industry relevant products

Essential Reading

1 .

M. L. Shuler and F. Kargi, Bioprocess Engineering: Basic Concepts, Prentice Hall of India, 2001

2 .

J E Bailey and D F Ollis, Biochemical Engineering Fundamentals, Mc Graw & Hills Publication

Supplementary Reading

1 .

P.M. Doran, Bioprocess Engineering Principles, Academic Press, 2012

2 .

B.W. Blanch and D. S Clark, Biochemical Engineering, Marcel Dekker Inc

Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : CS4107 : Optmization Techniques { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Origin, Characteristics and Techniques, operations research Modeling, Linear Programming Constraints with less than
equal to, equal to and greater than equal to types. The Simplex method, Dual simplex method, Revised simplex
method, Duality theory and sensitivity analysis. Transportation and Assignment problems, Traveling Salesman
problem using branch and bound method, Network analysis including PERT-CPM, Integer programming, Non-linear
programming problem solving using Fibonnacci search method, Golden ratio method, Gradient search method,
Gradient projection method and Hessian matrix method, Queuing theory and applications for different M/M/I and
M/M/C models. Inventory models considering holding cost, ordering cost and penalty costs.

Course Objective

1 .

To discuss the importance and usage of this course with real life examples.

Course Outcome

1 .

The students will know the scope of different optimization techniques.

Essential Reading

1 .

H. A. Taha, Operations Research an Introduction, Prentice Hall of India

2 .

F. S. Hillier, G. J. Lieberman, Introduction to Operation Research, Mc-Graw-Hill

Supplementary Reading

1 .

S. S. Rao, Optimisation Theory and applications, Wiley Eastern Ltd

2 .

B. E. Gillet, Introduction to Operation Research: a computer oriented algorithmic approach, Tata McGraw Hill

6090.b:
Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : CS6102 : Algorithm and Computational Complexity { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Algorithm and problem solving, Conventional algorithm design paradigms, Approximation Algorithms, Randomized Algorithms, Pattern matching algorithms, Lower bound Technique, Algebraic and number theoretic algorithms, Genetic Algorithms, Parallel Algorithms, Bioinformatics Algorithms
Easy and hard problems. Algorithms and complexity, Turing machines. Models of computation, Deterministic Complexity Classes, NP and NP-completeness. Non-deterministic Turing machines. Space complexity and hierarchy theorems. Optimization and approximation. Combinatorial optimisation problems. Polynomial and fully polynomial approximation schemes, Randomized Complexity

Course Objective

1 .

Analyze the asymptotic performance of algorithms
2 .

Write rigorous correctness proofs for algorithms
3 .

Apply important algorithmic design paradigms and methods of analysis.
4 .

Synthesize efficient algorithms in common engineering design situations.

Course Outcome

1 .

Analyze worst-case running times of algorithms using asymptotic analysis.
Describe the divide-and-conquer paradigm and explain when an algorithmic design situation calls for it. Recite algorithms that employ this paradigm. Synthesize divide-and-conquer algorithms. Derive and solve recurrences describing the performance of divide-and-conquer algorithms.
Describe the dynamic-programming paradigm and explain when an algorithmic design situation calls for it. Recite algorithms that employ this paradigm. Synthesize dynamic-programming algorithms, and analyze them.
Describe the greedy paradigm and explain when an algorithmic design situation calls for it. Recite algorithms that employ this paradigm. Synthesize greedy algorithms, and analyze them.
Explain the major graph algorithms and their analyses. Employ graphs to model engineering problems, when appropriate. Synthesize new graph algorithms and algorithms that employ graph computations as key components, and analyze them.
Explain the different ways to analyze randomized algorithms (expected running time, probability of error). Recite algorithms that employ randomization. Explain the difference between a randomized algorithm and an algorithm with probabilistic inputs.
Analyze randomized algorithms. Employ indicator random variables and linearity of expectation to perform the analyses. Recite analyses of algorithms that employ this method of analysis.
Explain what amortized running time is and what it is good for. Describe the different methods of amortized analysis (aggregate analysis, accounting, potential method). Perform amortized analysis.
Explain what competitive analysis is and to which situations it applies. Perform competitive analysis.
Compare between different data structures. Pick an appropriate data structure for a design situation.
Explain what an approximation algorithm is, and the benefit of using approximation algorithms. Be familiar with some approximation algorithms, including algorithms that are PTAS or FPTAS. Analyze the approximation factor of an algorithm.

Essential Reading

1 .

J Kleinberg, E Tardos, Algorithm Design, Addison-Wesley

2 .

Ellis Horowitz, Sartaj Sahni and Sanguthevar Rajasekaran., Fundamentals of Computer Algorithms, University Press

Supplementary Reading

1 .

T. H. Cormen, C. E. Leiserson, R. L. Rivest and C. Stein, Introduction to Algorithms, MIT Press

2 .

M. T. Goodrich and R. Tommassia, Algorithm Design, Wiley

19146.b:
Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : ME6173 : Rotodynamics and Turbomachinery Laboratory { 0-0-3 / 2}

Subject Nature : Practical

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Experiment 1. Rotordynamic analysis of rotor supported in rolling element bearings.
Experiment 2. Experiment on hydrodynamic bearings test rig.
Experiment 3. Prediction of expected life of a ball bearing for a corresponding load.
Experiment 4. Vibration studies of high speed locomotive turbocharger.
Experiment 5. Single plane balancing using industrial high precession balancing machine.
Experiment 6. Rotordynamics analysis of a misaligned rotor supported in rolling ellement bearings.
Experiment 7. Static and dynamic balancing of rotating masses.
Experiment 8. Rotordynamics analysis of a misaligned rotor supported in oil lubricated bearings.
Experiment 9. Vibration analysis of high speed cryogenic turboexpander
Experiment 10. Dual plane balancing using industrial high precession balancing machine.

Course Objective

1 .

Familiarize with the concept of rotordynamics studies to understand the behaviours of rotor supported in various types of bearings.
2 .

Get practical knowledge on various rotating machinery defects through vibration studies.
3 .

Learn to balance the unbalanced rotor using industrial balancing machines
4 .

Impart knowledge of various turbomachinery such as turbocharger and turboexpander.

Course Outcome

1 .

CO1: Understanding behaviours of rotor supported by various types of bearings.
CO2: Learn to acquire various signals data in rotor-bearing mechanical system in rotordynamic simulator .
CO3: learn to predict various defects in rotor-bearing mechanical system in rotordynamic simulator.
CO4: Understand behaviours of various high speed turbomachinery from vibration studies.
CO5: Understand concepts of unbalance and balancing methodology in balancing machine.

Essential Reading

1 .

Maurice L. Adams, Rotating Machinery Vibration: From Analysis to Troubleshooting, Second Edition (2nd ed.), CRC Press,2009, , https://doi.org/10.1201/9781439847558

2 .

Paresh Girdhar, C. Scheffer, Practical Machinery Vibration Analysis and Predictive Maintenance, Newnes,2004 , https://doi.org/10.1016/B978-075066275-8/50000-X

Supplementary Reading

1 .

John Vance, Fouad Zeidan, Brian Murphy, Machinery Vibration and Rotordynamics, John Wiley & Sons, Inc, 2010 , DOI:10.1002/9780470903704

2 .

John Vance, Rotordynamics of Turbomachinery, Wiley,1988 , ISBN:9780471802587, 0471802581

Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : MA5303 : Partial Differential Equations { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Origin of first-order partial differential equations, Cauchy’s problem, Linear equations, Integral surfaces passing through a given curve, Surfaces orthogonal to a given system of surfaces, Nonlinear partial differential equations of the first-order, Cauchy’s method of characteristics, Compatible systems of first-order equations, Charpit’s method, Jacobi’s method, Second and higher-order equations in physics, Linear partial differential equations, Characteristic curves, Separations of variables, Integral transform method for parabolic, hyperbolic and elliptic equations.

Course Objective

1 .

Partial differential equations allow deterministic mathematical formulations of phenomena in physics and engineering as well as biological processes among many other scenarios. The objective of this course is to present the main results in the context of partial differential equations that allow learning about these topics.
2 .

To equip students with the concepts of PDEs and how to solve PDEs with different analytical methods. Students also will be introduced to
some physical problems in Engineering models that result in PDEs.

Course Outcome

1 .

Apply logical/mathematical thinking: the analytic process. Apply some techniques/ methods to predict the behavior of certain phenomena. Identify real phenomena as models of PDEs.

Essential Reading

1 .

I. N. Sneddon, Elements of Partial Differential Equations, Dover Publications , 2006

2 .

S. J. Farlow, Partial Differential Equations for Scientists and Engineers, Dover Publications , 1993

Supplementary Reading

1 .

Tyn Myint-U and Lokenath Debnath, Linear Partial Differential Equations for Scientists and Engineers, Fourth Edition, Birkhauser , 2007

2 .

W.A. Strauss, Partial Differential Equations: An Introduction, John Wiley , 1992

8650.t: PA5416: Transgenerational and Gender-sensitive Neighbourhood Design
8650.b:
Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : PA5416 : Transgenerational and Gender-sensitive Neighbourhood Design { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module I (6 hours)
Global perspective on age-friendliness of cities and urban communities:
WHO on global age-friendly city guide Global strategy and action plan on ageing and health Social inclusion for an aging population Urban placemaking for elderly people Sustainable development and age-friendliness Best practices around the globe Theories and models - activity, subculture, disengagement, age-stratification, Ecological change, Environmental press, person-environment fit, Proactivity and reactivity, Walker’s theory on Active ageing.
Assignment: Term paper or seminars on case studies and best practices
Module II (6 hours)
Factors and parameters of age-friendliness of urban communities:
Identification of parameters based on the three strategic objectives set by WHO Various approaches adopted by researchers in identification of the same.
Assignment: Identification of factors and measurable indicators – literature review
Module III (6 hours)
Global perspective on child friendliness of cities and urban communities:
UNICEF’s vision on children in an urban area Child friendly cities and community’s handbook by WHO Drivers of child friendly cities Dimensions of child growth and effectiveness Infant Toddler and Caregiver (ITCN) friendliness Child rights Best practices Theories on the mental and physical development of infants, toddlers, young children, and impact of surrounding environment on them.
Assignment: Term paper or seminars on case studies and best practices
Module IV (6 hours)
Factors and parameters of child-friendliness of urban communities:
Identification and approaches for parameters based on child rights and their requirements.
Assignment: Identification of factors and measurable indicators – literature review
Module V (6 hours)
Gender equity in urban areas:
Defining society, men and women as members of society, understanding role of women in society, concepts in women empowerment, understanding gender sensitivity, theories of inclusive planning. Concept of gender-sensitive urban planning, understanding urban areas from women’s perspective, gender mainstreaming, gender budgeting, gender auditing, Gender Impact Assessment
Module VI (6 hours)
Global and other perspectives on gender sensitive urban and neighbourhood design:
Access to urban services, urban spaces, housing, ease of mobility, women in local governance, impact of climate change and other disasters on women, women’s role in sustainability, institutional mechanisms for gender equity in urban planning, best practices.
Assignment: Term paper or seminars on case studies and best practice.

Course Objective

1 .

To understand the necessity for age sensitive (age-friendly and child friendly) neighbourhood design.
2 .

To understand the necessity for gender sensitive neighbourhood design.
3 .

To analyse different approaches for designing transgenerational and gender sensitive neighbourhoods.

Course Outcome

1 .

1. An ability to develop an age-sensitive and gender sensitive perspective for neighbourhood design.
2. An ability to identify various factors and parameters explaining age-friendliness and child friendliness.
3. An ability to identify various factors and parameters for gender sensitive place making.
4. An ability to formulate a framework or methodological approach for designing transgenerational and gender sensitive neighbourhood.

Essential Reading

1 .

Bernard Van Leer Foundation (2019)., Infant-Toddler-Caregiver Friendly Neighbourhood Policy Framework, BVLF and NIUA

2 .

Moser, C. (2012)., Gender planning and development: Theory, practice and training., Routledge.

Supplementary Reading

1 .

Lobo, A., Camara, C. D., Garcia-Garcia, P. (2017)., Sociology of Aging. In H. Chiu and K. Shulman (Eds.), Mental Health and Illness of the Elderly, Mental Health and Illness Worldwide,, Springer

2 .

UN Human Settlements Programme (2012)., Gender and Urban Planning: Issues and Trends., United Nations

7882.t: SM6422: Total Quality Management and Six Sigma
7882.b:
Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : SM6422 : Total Quality Management and Six Sigma { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Principles of TQM: TQM Framework, Service Quality Model, Supplier Management, Contributions of Deming, Juran Crosby, Ishikawa, Feigenbaum, Taguchi Techniques, Parameter and Tolerance Design. Statistical Process Control: Statistical concepts, Control Charts for Variables and Attributes Process Capability, Reliability Concepts. Measurement systems evaluation Tools and Techniques of Quality Management: Seven New Management Tools, Japanese Techniques, Principles and Methodology, Quality Functions Deployment (QFD), Failure Mode Effect Analysis (FMEA), Benchmarking. Quality Systems: Quality Circles, Quality Management Systems, ISO Certifications, Quality Audits, TQM Culture. Six Sigma Interface: Six Sigma Philosophy, Linking Six Sigma Projects to Strategies, Attributes of Good Metrics, Tracking Six Sigma Project Results, Six Sigma Teams.

Course Objective

1 .

To enrich the fundamentals of Total Quality Management to foster the emerging trends in production whereby students practically would know how the six sigma technique could be used to minimize defects.

Course Outcome

1 .

This course is designed to enrich the fundamentals of Total Quality Management to foster the emerging trends in production whereby students practically would know how the six sigma technique could be used to minimize defects.

Essential Reading

Besterfield, D. H. (2003), Total Quality Management., Prentice Hall

2 .

Pyzdek, T., and Keller, P. (2010)., The Six Sigma Handbook (3rded.), Tata McGraw - Hill Education

Supplementary Reading

Goetsch, D. L., Stanley, B. D. (2012)., Quality Management for Organizational Excellence: Introduction to Total Quality (7thed.)., Prentice Hall PTR.
